title: Phrasing in practice
goal: Worked examples, what it saves, and what the grammar leaves out.

blocks.x: Steno order: left bank (starter), vowels and star, right bank. With no vowels or star, `-` marks the start of the right bank, as in {{I am}} [[SWR-B]].

Hold `#` (the number bar) with any phrase and it comes out as a question: the auxiliary first, then the starter. [[you can|KPWRA]] is *you can*; [[can you|#KPWRA]] is the same stroke plus `#`. Nothing else changes: starter, vowels, star and verb are where they were.

Only an auxiliary can open a question, so a plain verb takes *do*: *you think* becomes *do you think*, *he said* becomes *did he say*, *I have* becomes *do I have*. *have been* keeps its *have* (*have I been*). Twenty common questions already have their own stroke and keep it: [[do you|UD]], [[are you|R*U]], [[can we|KWAOE]], [[is there|STHR*]]. *what*, *how* and *why* are their own stroke, then the question: two strokes. Details and the full list: [questions](#/ref/phrases/questions).
*there* takes *be*, *have been* and the modals only, not the other verbs, and no bare *do*: [[there is|STHR-B]], [[there was|STHREB]], [[there would be|STHROEB]], [[there must have been|STHRAUFB]].
Where it sits in the dictionary

The generator fixes the grammar's 3,758 strokes before any word settles, as it does the suffix strokes, so every one is placed and a word whose own candidates landed on one took its next outline: 122 words changed an outline, and of the 5,000 commonest only {{pity}} and {{impress}} moved their primary. The merged two-word phrases leave the texts the grammar writes to it (*it is* is [[it is|KPWH-B]]). Every word keeps an outline. The 3,738 question strokes (`#` plus a statement's keys) are placed last, after the merged pairs and every word: the bar is free on all of them and a question that already has an entry keeps it.

Measured by `python3 tools/phrasing_prototype.py --savings BEFORE` against a build made without the grammar, the merged two-word phrases counted in both. The novels are third-person past narration; everyday first- and second-person present typing has more of these pairs per word, so this undercounts: the extracted quote passages of the test corpus, which are speech, spend 17% fewer strokes with phrases and grammar than word by word. The question forms add a little on top: 1,014 fewer strokes on the novels (0.17%), none on these quote passages. They pay off in speech and messages (*can you* is in about one message in eleven of the author's), not in narration.

lyk lookup "they wouldn't"
lyk lookup "I do not know"
lyk lookup SWRAB

The lookup puts the grammar's stroke first, with the key group that says each part (`STWHR starter (they) + OE auxiliary (would) + * not`), then each word on its own. Given a stroke it says which phrase it is. The site's Lookup does the same; details: [looking a phrase up](#/ref/phrases/looking-a-phrase-up).
